note: Great shot of these blooming by Alaina, one of our high school volunteers! The mass planting outside the office is at times unruly, so we enjoy them now while we can.
quick_hits: Look between the red bracts: the slim orange tubes with dark tips are the actual flowers, and on this heliconia they are half the show.
Each flower opens just before dawn and has stopped making nectar by early afternoon.
In Brazil a skipper butterfly pollinates it before sunrise, alongside hummingbirds and an orchid bee.

note: A cornsnake surprised us at the Team Workday by jumping out from our pond plants into the water! Harmless, handsome, and colorful! Susan was unphased, and Randy re-thought going into the waters to plant native cannas.
quick_hits: Orange, red or brown blotches edged in black run along its orange-brown body. Adults commonly reach about two and a half to four feet.
It climbs well and hunts mainly at night.

note: Patty spotted this sphinx moth- first recorded at the park! A fast flyer that hovers at flowers like a hummingbird, so look at dusk.
quick_hits: A slim, sharply pointed moth that flies at dusk, hovering at flowers to drink nectar through a long tongue, much like a hummingbird.
Its caterpillars feed on pentas and firebush, both of which grow here.
The caterpillar carries a row of eyespots along its sides. Alarmed, it pulls its head in and puffs up its front end so the spots stare back.

note: Franky and her team planted this tree in September to replace a sadly fallen baobab from the storms of past years. We also lost a rainbow eucalyptus near the cactus garden, so this is a welcome back of sorts!
quick_hits: The bark peels away in strips. The fresh bark underneath is bright green, and it darkens through blues, purples and oranges as it ages.
Unlike most eucalyptus, it comes from rainforest, not dry Australian bush.
On Maui, a roadside grove of these trees is one of the famous stops on the Road to Hana.

note: Unexpected Helping Hand. Photographer Helen Lewis spotted something remarkable: a Northern Cardinal feeding a young Northern Mockingbird chick. A wonderful little moment of unexpected care, caught right here at the park.
quick_hits: Males are bright red with a pointed crest and black face mask; females are warm buff-brown with red tinges. Both carry the same stout orange-red bill.
Both sexes sing. In many North American songbirds only the male does.
That heavy conical bill is a seed-cracker, opening tough seeds many birds cannot manage.

note: This is the best time of year to see Beautyberry in its full purple. Like a Dr Seuss plant!
area: Near Office and around Cypress Pond
quick_hits: Around the beginning of September, tight clusters of vivid purple fruit appear directly around the stems. At Palma Sola, that is when Beautyberry suddenly seems to be everywhere.
American Beautyberry is a Florida native. Ours grow around Cypress Pond and the office, and some appear to have seeded themselves into new spots.
The fruit is edible, though fresh Beautyberries are tart and not especially flavorful; they are more often made into jelly, with a lot of sugar.
